article_title: EveryDay Intervention (Family Engagement)
citation: Attendance. (2018). https://www.evidenceforlearning.org
title: Attendance interventions can be delivered at scale with minimal staffing, training, and technology
description: The page specifies that the Absence Reports intervention requires minimal staffing — one district staff member supporting implementation at approximately 30 minutes per week and one district-level data staff member supporting data transfer in under 3 hours total — and that professional development is minimal, with "none required aside from the staffing requirements described above," and no technology required. This shows a low-burden delivery model can accompany a statistically significant attendance effect, making district adoption feasible without extensive training infrastructure.
requirements: One district staff member for implementation support and one district-level data staff member for data transfer
constraints: Staffing estimates are as printed for this program; the page does not generalize them to other interventions
target_learners: District and school staff implementing attendance interventions
target_learning_goals: Reducing student absences through feasible district-level implementation
examples: The program's stated staffing is one district staff member at approximately 30 min/week plus one data staff member contributing under 3 hours of total work.

article_title: Menu of Measures: High-Quality Measures of Middle Years Math Student Outcomes

description: The menu organizes measurement of middle grades math outcomes into three domains: students' "math skills and knowledge", "math perceptions and beliefs", and "math use beyond the classroom". This taxonomy lets educators, district leaders, researchers, and funders select measures spanning performance, dispositions, and out-of-school engagement rather than achievement alone.

math attitudes and beliefs
math engagement beyond the classroom
examples: The resource's summary lists the three domains as the scope of its curated measures

article_title: A View from the Elementary Schools
citation: Bryk, A. S., Easton, J. Q., Kerbow, D., Rollow, S. G., & Sebring, P. A. (1993). A View from the Elementary Schools: The State of Reform in Chicago. Consortium on Chicago School Research.
title: Judge urban school reform mid-course by organizational direction, not short-term achievement trends
description: The report argues that a mid-course assessment of a systemic urban reform should examine whether ongoing organizational rearrangements are occurring and whether new arrangements operate as planned, rather than judging by short-term test-score changes. It reasons that "short-term profits might plummet as losses are incurred in the process of reshaping the basic mission and operating procedures," and that even the best cases of significant individual school improvement often required five or more years to culminate in comprehensive restructuring.
requirements: An assessment framework organized around the reform's own theory of change, in this case enhanced participation as a lever for improvement
constraints: The report explicitly rejects the legislation's 1994 national-norms timetable as not defensible for a system of over 400,000 students and 25,000 teachers
target_learners: Students in large urban school systems undergoing systemic reform
target_learning_goals: Improving student learning through governance restructuring and instructional improvement
examples: The report redirects its evaluative questions toward how new governance structures function, what types of improvement efforts are underway, and whether participation provides an effective lever for improvement
key_sources: Bryk, A. S., Easton, J. Q., Kerbow, D., Rollow, S. G., & Sebring, P. A. (1993). A View from the Elementary Schools: The State of Reform in Chicago. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/view-elementary-schools-state-reform-chicago

article_title: The Influence of Rapidly Guessed Item Responses on Teacher Value-Added Estimates: Implications for Policy and Practice
citation: Andrew Rice. (2018). The influence of rapidly guessed item responses on teacher value-added estimates: Implications for policy and practice. Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis, 40(2), 267-284. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=The+influence+of+rapidly+guessed+item+responses+on+teacher+value-added+estimates
title: Educators should be mindful of rapid guessing when interpreting student test results
description: The article recommends that because rapid guessing occurs frequently on achievement tests, educators should attend to its presence when interpreting what student test scores mean. The authors state that "rapid guessing occurs frequently enough that educators should be mindful of its effect on the interpretations of student test results." This recommendation follows from their finding that the behavior varies across grades, subjects, and teachers, even though it did not substantively change teacher value-added estimates under their specifications.
requirements: Test response-time or rapid-guessing behavior must be observable or estimable for the test results being interpreted.
constraints: The article's own value-added analysis found no substantive effect of rapid guessing on teacher performance estimates under the specifications used, so the recommendation concerns score interpretation rather than teacher accountability estimates.
target_learning_goals: Valid interpretation of student achievement test results
examples: The study examined rapid guessing prevalence on achievement tests and evaluated its influence on teacher value-added estimates before recommending mindful interpretation.
key_sources: Andrew Rice. (2018). The influence of rapidly guessed item responses on teacher value-added estimates: Implications for policy and practice. Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis, 40(2), 267-284. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=The+influence+of+rapidly+guessed+item+responses+on+teacher+value-added+estimates

article_title: Looking beyond vision: Supports for students who are blind or visually impaired in mathematics
citation: Steinbach, S. (2022). Looking beyond vision: Supports for students who are blind or visually impaired in mathematics. NWEA.
title: Provide BVI students with a mixed-representational, multi-sensory approach to mathematical materials
description: The review argues that because there is not a "one size fits all" way of presenting technical information, mathematical materials for BVI students should combine multiple representations and senses — tactile, verbal, tonal, haptic — rather than relying on a single access mode. It cites evidence that combining voiced auditory descriptions with tactile graphics increased braille readers' likelihood of correct answers, and that successful approaches "provide a variety of interfaces for access". Adapted materials act as a bridge from sequential perception to more well-rounded understanding.
requirements: Materials must be adapted for BVI use, since BVI students perceive the world through tactile and acoustic inputs in a sequential way at first
constraints: More research is needed on the effects of a multisensory approach on math task performance and on how to teach BVIs to gather information from multiple sources efficiently
target_learners: Students who are blind or visually impaired in K-12 mathematics
target_learning_goals: Accessing and demonstrating mathematical content knowledge through non-visual and multi-sensory representations
examples: The review cites Ferrell et al. (2017) preliminary results showing braille readers with both voiced auditory descriptions and tactile graphics increased their likelihood of answering items correctly
key_sources: Steinbach, S. (2022). Looking beyond vision: Supports for students who are blind or visually impaired in mathematics. NWEA. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/looking-beyond-vision-supports-for-students-who-are-blind-or-visually-impaired-in-mathematics/

article_title: Research and Development in America's Schools
citation: Smith, K. A., & Stewart, J. (2026, January). Research and development in America’s schools: How school systems drive sustainable improvement and innovation. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/283
title: Micro-R&D: teachers test new tools and ideas on a small scale before successful practices enter the broader curriculum
description: At South Fayette Township School District (PA), R&D operates as a culture of experimentation rather than a department. The report describes that "This approach empowers teachers to test new tools and ideas on a small scale, often in after-school clubs, summer programs, or elective courses, before integrating successful practices into the broader curriculum." Success is measured by student interest and engagement—elective signups, club attendance, word-of-mouth—rather than standardized metrics, with leadership intentionally flat and distributed so teachers, students, and community members co-design programs.
requirements: Leadership trust, autonomy, and strategic risk-taking; administrators acting as facilitators connecting educators to grants and partners
constraints: The report notes traditional data may be sparse in this approach, with engagement indicators serving as evidence of impact
target_learners: K-12 students in a suburban district; teachers as innovators
target_learning_goals: Iterative local innovation in curriculum and programs, student engagement and interest
examples: Programs cited include drone academies, vertical horticulture, blockchain courses, esports, and Mini-THON
key_sources: Smith, K. A., & Stewart, J. (2026, January). Research and development in America’s schools: How school systems drive sustainable improvement and innovation. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/283

article_title: Micro-credentials: Driving teacher learning & leadership
citation: Barnett Berry and Karen Cator. (2016). Micro-credentials: Driving teacher learning & leadership. Center for Teaching Quality and Digital Promise. http://teachingquality.org/micro-credentials
title: Four key characteristics of the micro-credential approach: competency-based, personalized, on-demand, shareable
description: The report identifies four characteristics distinguishing micro-credentials from traditional professional development. They are "Competency-based," focusing on "evidence of educators’ actual skills and abilities, not the amount of 'seat time'"; personalized, with teachers selecting credentials based on their own needs and contexts; on-demand, responsive to teachers' schedules through an agile online system; and shareable as "portable currency for professional learning" across platforms, résumés, and blogs. Each micro-credential specifies what the teacher should know and do, recommends resources, and specifies the evidence required to demonstrate competence.
requirements: Each micro-credential must provide a competency definition, recommended resources, and a specification of the evidence an educator must submit
constraints: The report notes implementing micro-credentials will not guarantee teachers have the time they need to collaborate and learn together
target_learning_goals: demonstrating discrete professional competencies
personalized professional growth
examples: Teachers identify a credential, pursue learning at a time and location they choose, gather and submit evidence such as portfolios, video, student work, or classroom observations, and earn a digital badge
key_sources: Barnett Berry and Karen Cator. (2016). Micro-credentials: Driving teacher learning & leadership. Center for Teaching Quality and Digital Promise. http://teachingquality.org/micro-credentials

article_title: Micro-credentials for Impact: Holding Professional Learning to High Standards
citation: Crow, T. (contributing author Pipkin, H.). (2017). Micro-credentials for Impact: Holding Professional Learning to High Standards. Learning Forward and Digital Promise. https://www.digitalpromise.org/micro-credentials
title: Require evidence of authentic classroom application so micro-credential learning is practiced and sustained
description: Under the Implementation standard, the report argues that professional learning must be sustained and supported through practice, coaching, and feedback, and notes that micro-credentials support this because they are competency-based and evidence-driven: "Because micro-credentials in most instances require evidence of application, they require practice of new learning." Issuers are advised to build in practice opportunities before evidence submission and require student work samples where appropriate.
requirements: Intentional resources and structures that give adult learners opportunities to follow up their learning through practice, coaching, and constructive feedback
constraints: Learning aligned with the Implementation standard isn't one-time or episodic but sustained and intensive
target_learning_goals: sustained implementation of new instructional strategies and lessons in classrooms
examples: Recommendations include providing coaches and time for team practice and sharing lessons learned and exemplary evidence from the assessment process
key_sources: Crow, T. (contributing author Pipkin, H.). (2017). Micro-credentials for Impact: Holding Professional Learning to High Standards. Learning Forward and Digital Promise. https://www.digitalpromise.org/micro-credentials

article_title: Designing for the future of research: Putting equity-relevant research into practice with scenarios and personas
citation: Pakhira, D., & Fusco, J. (2022, October). Designing for the future of research: Putting equity-relevant research into practice with scenarios and personas. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/163
title: Minimize bias in learning platforms by diversifying the developers, training data, and feedback sources behind algorithms
description: The article's third recommendation addresses algorithmic bias: any algorithm has the potential to be biased because it reflects the biases of the humans who develop and validate it. It recommends ensuring that algorithms and training data represent diverse learners by including developers with diverse backgrounds who use their lived experiences to shape algorithms in terms of race, ethnicity, gender, and nationality, plus feedback from parents, students, and teachers in communities where the algorithm will be used.
requirements: Developers with diverse backgrounds and perspectives shaping the algorithms
Feedback from parents, students, and teachers who represent communities where the algorithm will be used
constraints: Machine learning systems working with student data can learn biases from technical design errors and from existing patterns of inequality and discrimination in training data
Readily available data leads to overrepresentation of specific subsets of the population
target_learners: students in communities where platform algorithms are deployed
target_learning_goals: preventing algorithmic bias from influencing student learner performance and behavior
examples: The article cites studies on educational AI reflecting on origins of AI bias and potential harms in education

title: For students who decode well but comprehend poorly, minimize decoding and fluency instruction and maximize comprehension instruction
description: The panel advises differentiating intervention content by profile: students who read multisyllabic words effortlessly but perform poorly on reading tests because of weak vocabulary and comprehension difficulties need language work, not more decoding. "Teachers should minimize decoding and fluency instruction and maximize comprehension instruction." These students should be grouped into interventions focused on oral language and reading comprehension.
requirements: Group these students in an intervention focusing on oral language and reading comprehension
Include activities that increase world knowledge and word knowledge with meaningful discussion of texts
constraints: Students who demonstrate mastery of both simple and advanced letter combinations do not need a word-reading intervention, though they may benefit from vocabulary and comprehension remediation

target_learning_goals: Oral language development and reading comprehension
examples: The panel's obstacle advice recommends including words from core subject-area classes during intervention time, such as Reconstruction and suffrage for a Civil War unit

article_title: MAP Reading Fluency with Coach: Evidence Base
citation: MAP Reading Fluency with Coach Evidence Base. (2024). NWEA. https://www.nwea.org
title: Microintervention scaffolds delivered at word, phrase, and story levels during oral reading practice
description: Coach delivers scaffolded support as responses to errors detected during oral reading, at three moments within a reading session: word level when a student is stuck on a word, phrase level when a student misreads words within a sentence, and story level as a wrap-up building comprehension at the end of the story. Each microintervention is described as a "scaffold" aligned to the Reading Rope, with dozens employed to build foundational reading skills in English and Spanish.
requirements: Automated speech recognition to detect oral reading errors in real time; assessment data identifying skills needing work toward mastery
constraints: Microinterventions respond to errors in oral reading of connected text; they are delivered within the tutoring session rather than as separate lessons
target_learners: K-5 emerging readers using the Coach tutoring pathway
target_learning_goals: foundational reading skills
decoding
fluency
comprehension
examples: Real-time microinterventions include reading along, lip-syncing, and rhyming words that strengthen critical foundational skills.

article_title: District and school leaders’ perspectives on leading & learning during the COVID-19 pandemic
citation: Hayley Weddle, Ayesha K. Hashim, Ogechi Irondi. (2022). District and school leaders’ perspectives on leading & learning during the COVID-19 pandemic. Education Policy Innovation Collaborative. https://epicedpolicy.org/district-leaders-perspectives-on-the-covid19-pandemic/
title: Return to Learn legislation framework for studying pandemic learning in Michigan
description: Michigan's Return to Learn legislation (2020 PA 147, 148, 149) tasked the Michigan Department of Education with "studying student progress toward learning goals during and beyond the 2020-21 school year." It also directed understanding "how schools were effective at meeting educational goals and attainment across in-person, hybrid, and remote instructional modalities." The EPIC study of district responses operationalizes this legislative mandate, using leaders' perspectives to surface best practices for supporting student learning during COVID-19.
requirements: State legislation mandating study of student progress and school effectiveness across instructional modalities
constraints: Applies to Michigan districts and the period during and beyond the 2020-21 school year
target_learners: K-12 students in Michigan school districts
target_learning_goals: Progress toward learning goals; educational goal attainment across instructional modalities
examples: The EPIC study at Michigan State University conducts this research in response to the Return to Learn legislation

article_title: Catching up or falling behind: Measuring middle school achievement trajectories for college readiness
citation: Angela Johnson, Megan Kuhfeld, and Greg King. (2020). Catching up or Falling Behind: Measuring Middle School Achievement Trajectories for College Readiness. EdWorkingPaper No. 20-233, Annenberg Institute at Brown University.
title: Trajectory-based early indicator framework monitoring on-track status for college readiness across middle school
description: The article presents a framework that applies college readiness benchmarks to longitudinal middle-grades assessment data, assigning each student a series of up to six on-track status indicators and grouping students into six trajectory patterns. As the authors state, this study demonstrates an early academic indicator approach that continuously monitors students' on-track status from the beginning of 6th grade to the end of 8th grade. The framework identifies when achievement growth acceleration and deceleration happen using vertically scaled scores.
requirements: At least one test score in each grade between 6th and 8th grade (fall of 6th, fall or spring of 7th, spring of 8th) to construct a full trajectory
constraints: The analyses are descriptive, and the estimates should not be taken as causal links
The GRD sample may not be nationally representative
target_learning_goals: Academic college readiness in math and reading
examples: Applied to 363,685 students in 5,900 schools, organizing trajectories into six groups: three who start on-track and three who start off-track

article_title: The Essential Playbook for Family Engagement in Middle School
citation: Wallace, M., & Paredes, M. (2024). The essential playbook for family engagement in middle school. WestEd. https://www.wested.org

article_title: Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Take Ownership over Their Learning with Formative Assessment
citation: Barbara Jones, Molly Faulkner-Bond, and Jennifer Blitz. (2024). Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Take Ownership Over Their Learning With Formative Assessment. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: Middle school transition-words writing lesson integrating self-assessment, peer feedback, and personal learning goals
description: A middle school lesson vignette in which English learners and native English-speaking students learn to show relationships between ideas by combining sentences with transition words. Students write personal learning goals based on the success criterion, revise drafts with optional partner brainstorming and sentence stems, exchange peer feedback aligned to the success criteria, rate themselves using a rubric, and set a new personal learning goal for the next lesson.
requirements: The teacher designed the lesson after reviewing students' writing drafts from a previous day, which demonstrated that students needed support creating coherence and fluidity in their writing.
target_learners: Middle school English learners at various proficiency levels and native English-speaking peers
target_learning_goals: Using transition words to show relationships between ideas in writing (time order, place, compare and contrast, cause and effect, importance)
examples: After receiving peer feedback, students assess their own writing based on the success criterion and their personal learning goal, and the teacher plans to review students' self-assessments and personal goals to inform lesson planning.

article_title: Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Take Ownership over Their Learning with Formative Assessment
citation: Barbara Jones, Molly Faulkner-Bond, and Jennifer Blitz. (2024). Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Take Ownership Over Their Learning With Formative Assessment. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: Middle school biotechnology fermented-drinks lesson demonstrating asset-based instruction and divergent formative assessment
description: A snapshot vignette of a middle school science lesson in which English learners at various proficiency levels work with non-English learner peers to apply biotechnology principles: researching fermented drinks made by family members and neighbors, creating one from an existing family recipe, and developing an original drink for a local target audience. A student's aunt shares her fermentation expertise, and the teacher checks in with groups, asking open-ended questions and providing feedback.
requirements: Each subsequent task in the lesson builds on the prior one to move students toward the learning goal, making learning visible to the teacher and fellow students and providing actionable evidence for formulating next steps.
target_learners: Middle school English learners at various levels of English proficiency and their non-English learner peers
target_learning_goals: Applying principles of biotechnology to real-world situations
examples: After reviewing taste-survey results, students decided to switch their flavor choice to reflect only one target audience; the teacher's open-ended question "How can you find out?" prompted them to draw on peers' research displayed around the room, supporting individual and group agency.

article_title: The Impact of the Mindsets Mathematics Program on Student Engagement, Ability to Reason, and Repeated Reasoning
citation: Gage, N. (2025). The impact of the Mindsets mathematics program on student engagement, ability to reason, and repeated reasoning. WestEd. https://WestEd.org
title: Mindsets mathematics program: collaborative, hands-on, challenge-based curriculum aligned to the Standards for Mathematical Practice
description: Mindsets is a mathematics program built around "collaborative, hands-on challenges that immerse students in real-world scenarios." Each multi-hour challenge opens with a compelling real-life context, moves students through increasingly complex problems highlighting a particular SMP, and ends with a culminating hands-on activity such as making pancakes or setting prices for a dog-walking business. Teachers receive targeted professional development and real-time implementation support, and challenges align with the California Mathematics Framework without being California-specific.

ability to reason abstractly and quantitatively (SMP 2)
repeated reasoning (SMP 8)
examples: In the 2025 summer session, challenges were organized around weekly themes: Building Community, Food Week, Movement, Shark Tank, and The Amazing Race

article_title: Developing a System of Micro-credentials: Supporting Deeper Learning in the Classroom
citation: Developing a System of Micro-credentials: Supporting Deeper Learning in the Classroom. (2014). Digital Promise. https://www.digitalpromise.org/microcredentials
title: Eight design characteristics of micro-credentials
description: The article enumerates the design characteristics of educator micro-credentials: they are "Bite-sized—focused on a specific, observable competency," subject-adaptable, research-based, teacher- and student-centered, personal and timely, portable as digital badges, transparent with publicly available assessment criteria, and performance-based. This list defines the reusable instructional design pattern the credential system follows, specifying how each credential is scoped, evidenced, and shared so that professional learning can be recognized in competency-based rather than time-based terms.
requirements: Each micro-credential targets a specific, observable competency and is demonstrated through artifacts with publicly available assessment criteria
target_learners: practicing K-12 teachers and professional educators
target_learning_goals: earning recognition for specific teaching competencies aligned to student needs
examples: Micro-credentials can be shared as digital badges in online platforms and adapted to multiple subject areas

article_title: Certifying Competencies and Skills with Micro-credentials in a Global Context
citation: Rita Fennelly-Atkinson and April Williamson (Digital Promise). (2023). Certifying Competencies and Skills with Micro-credentials in a Global Context. Digital Promise presentation. https://digitalpromise.org/microcredentials
title: Micro-credentials as digital credentials verifying competence in a skill or set of skills

licensure and recertification
professional learning application
examples: Digital Promise launched its Micro-credential Platform in 2015 with 100 micro-credentials and awarded its first micro-credential the same year

article_title: El Rol de las Micro-credenciales en el Aprendizaje y el Desarrollo a lo Largo de la Vida: Empoderando Estudiantes, Empoderando Organizaciones
citation: Galindo, M., Fennelly-Atkinson, R., Franklin, K., Luna, C. (2024). El Rol de las Micro-credenciales en el Aprendizaje y el Desarrollo a lo Largo de la Vida: Empoderando Estudiantes, Empoderando Organizaciones. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/233
title: Taxonomía del ecosistema de credenciales: macro-credenciales versus micro-credenciales basadas en competencias
description: El eBook organiza el ecosistema de credenciales en dos grandes ramas: macro-credenciales (títulos y certificados universitarios y de posgrado) y micro-credenciales, definidas como credenciales digitales que "verifica la competencia en una destreza o conjunto de destrezas específicas". Según la definición de UNESCO citada, una micro-credencial es un registro de logros de aprendizaje focalizados con evaluación basada en estándares claramente definidos, otorgada por un proveedor de confianza, con valor independiente y sujeta a garantía de calidad. El eBook enfatiza que las micro-credenciales no son programas de aprendizaje sino reconocimiento de la capacidad de aplicar lo aprendido, independientemente de cómo se adquirió.
requirements: Evaluación basada en estándares claramente definidos y otorgada por un proveedor de confianza
constraints: En este eBook, las micro-credenciales no son un programa de aprendizaje o adiestramiento, sino que representan la capacidad de aplicar el aprendizaje y el conocimiento
target_learners: Estudiantes de todas las edades, incluyendo educadores K-12, estudiantes postsecundarios y trabajadores

article_title: Simulating Students or Sycophantic Problem Solving? On Misconception Faithfulness of LLM Simulators
citation: Heejin Do, Shashank Sonkar, Mrinmaya Sachan. (2026). Simulating Students or Sycophantic Problem Solving? On Misconception Faithfulness of LLM Simulators. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.12748
title: Misconception faithfulness framework: misconception-contrastive feedback protocol and Selective Flip Score
description: The article proposes a diagnostic framework evaluating whether an LLM student simulator "preserves misconception-consistent belief state and selectively updates it only when feedback addresses the underlying misconception." Its core is a misconception-contrastive feedback protocol comparing targeted feedback (addressing the true misconception), misaligned feedback (targeting a different plausible misconception), and generic feedback (only signaling incorrectness), from which the Selective Flip Score SFS = FT − ½(FM + FG) quantifies selective sensitivity. The framework also includes a six-category student response taxonomy distinguishing content-sensitive updates (correct flip, constructive pushback) from content-insensitive ones (sycophantic flip, passive maintain).

Feedback conditions must isolate semantic alignment as the primary source of variation
constraints: The framework focuses on mathematics domains with misconceptions drawn from existing taxonomies; extending to less structured domains remains future work
SFS measures observable behavioral updates rather than latent belief states directly
Teacher feedback and response classifications are generated by LLMs rather than human-authored
target_learners: LLM-based student simulators used to train and evaluate AI tutors and human educators
target_learning_goals: Diagnosing and responding to misconception-driven student reasoning during tutoring interaction
examples: The framework was applied to seven instruction-tuned LLMs (4B–120B) on the Malrule and EEDI datasets under base and reflective prompting, and used as the reward basis for SFT, DPO, and GRPO post-training.

citation: Doyle C, Smeaton AF, Roche RAP and Boran L (2018) Inhibition and Updating, but Not Switching, Predict Developmental Dyslexia and Individual Variation in Reading Ability. Front. Psychol. 9:795. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2018.00795
title: Miyake and Friedman's 3-factor model of core executive functions (inhibition, updating, switching)
description: The article organizes its profiling study around the 3-factor model of executive function, in which executive function comprises three core related but separable abilities. It states that "Inhibition is deﬁned as the ability to override inappropriate responses, regulate appropriate behaviour and control attenti on by focusing on relevant information and ﬁltering out distracting information; updating is the ability to hold and continuousl y update information in working memory from moment to moment; and switching is the ability to rapidly adapt to changing task demands." The model holds that the three are related through a common executive function (inhibition) while updating and switching are specific, and that complex tasks lack the specificity to detect fine-grained core processes. The study applies this framework to dyslexia using multiple measures per construct.

citation: Dweck, C. S., & Yeager, D. S. (2019). Mindsets: A View From Two Eras. Perspectives on Psychological Science. https://doi.org/10.1177/1745691618804166
title: Mindset meaning-system framework: fixed versus growth mindsets organize goals, effort beliefs, attributions, and persistence
description: The meaning-system framework holds that mindsets are not isolated beliefs but organizing structures that link goals, effort beliefs, attributions, and persistence into a coherent system. constraints: The article notes a growth mindset is not always positive: persistence without progress should be questioned, and a growth mindset can be used for negative ends.

persistence and resilience after setbacks
academic achievement

citation: Liang, C., Toyokawa, Y., & Ogata, H. (2025). Optimizing group formation with a mixed genetic algorithm: an empirical study in active reading using marker data. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09452-9
title: Mixed genetic algorithm fitness function balancing homogeneous and heterogeneous grouping components
description: The article adapts a mixed genetic algorithm (inspired by Revelo Sanchez et al., 2021) for data-driven group formation. The score is interpretable in relative terms, not as an absolute indicator

description: The review conceptually integrates mind wandering with SRL frameworks (COPES; MASRL), arguing that "mind wandering should not be viewed merely as a disruption of SRL but rather as an integral process that interacts with cognitive, metacognitive, motivational, and affective regulation." It distinguishes subtypes by meta-awareness — "one without awareness (zone-outs) and one with awareness (tune-outs)" — and by intentionality. Unaware mind wandering signals a lapse in metacognitive monitoring, whereas aware, intentional mind wandering may function as an affective or motivational regulation strategy, e.g., managing frustration or sustaining engagement.
requirements: Researchers must precisely specify which subtype of mind wandering (by meta-awareness and intentionality) they study
constraints: The review focuses on the performance phase of SRL models, where most mind-wandering studies examine task-unrelated thoughts
target_learning_goals: metacognitive monitoring
affect and motivation regulation during learning
examples: The review describes learners deliberately allowing their minds to wander to manage heightened frustration, reflecting on pleasant or rewarding thoughts to stabilize their emotional state.

Mapping Mind Wandering to the “Self-Regulated Learning Process, Multimodal Data, and Analysis Grid”: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10041-3

article_title: The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity
citation: Smagorinsky, P., & Smith, M. W. (1992). The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity. Review of Educational Research, 62(3), 279-305. http://rer.aera.net
title: Foster mindful attention to transfer by systematically saturating instruction with attention to transfer
description: Drawing on Perkins and Salomon, the review recommends that teachers who want knowledge to transfer across domains make transfer an explicit, conscious object of instruction. Teachers who "persistently and systematically . . . saturate the context of education with attention to transfer" improve the likelihood that students will reapply knowledge when they shift domains. This saturation must be integral to class structure rather than a tag at the end of a lesson.
requirements: Consistent mindfulness must be fostered in students adapting knowledge to new situations
constraints: Salomon found most students are decidedly unmindful unless specifically and vigorously cued
target_learners: students in composition and literary understanding instruction
target_learning_goals: applying knowledge in contexts other than the one originally studied
examples: The review presents this as hope for teachers adopting the community-specific knowledge position who aspire to retain influence on student writing

article_title: A systematic review of the key components of online peer feedback practices in higher education
citation: Xingshi Gao, Omid Noroozi, Judith Gulikers, Harm J.A. Biemans, Seyyed Kazem Banihashem. (2024). A systematic review of the key components of online peer feedback practices in higher education. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100588
title: The MISCA model as a five-component framework for evaluating feedback practices
description: The review adopts the MISCA (Message, Implementation, Student Characteristics, Context, Agents) model proposed by Panadero and Lipnevich (2022), which integrates five common components for classifying feedback practices: Content, Function, Student Characteristics, Presentation, and Source. The article states that "The model shows the complexity of feedback process and provides a theoretical framework for understanding and evaluating the key components that influence feedback practices." Student Characteristics is placed at the center of the model as "the unique component that influences the other four." The review uses these five components as the deductive coding scheme for analyzing online peer feedback studies.
requirements: The framework requires analyzing feedback practices across all five components (content, function, student characteristics, presentation, source) rather than in isolation
constraints: The review applies the model to written peer feedback comments in online or blended higher-education settings
target_learning_goals: improving task performance through peer feedback
feedback quality and uptake
examples: The review coded 73 articles deductively under the five MISCA components, producing Tables 3–7 of categories and sub-categories

article_title: Learning by Doing or Doing Without Learning? The Potentials and Challenges of Activity-Based Learning
citation: Alexander Skulmowski. (2024). Learning by Doing or Doing Without Learning? The Potentials and Challenges of Activity-Based Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09869-y
title: Design activity-based learning to avoid redundant demands and provide guidance, favoring biologically primary activity components
description: The review recommends that if activity-based interventions are used, designers should strip out redundant aspects, supply guidance, and shift focus toward low-demand components. It states that "as many redundant aspects as possible need to be avoided while providing additional guidance to learners," and that learning activities "may be more effective if the extraneous task demands are removed and the focus is shifted towards the less demanding components, such as gesturing." Guidance for drawing and restricting drawing to easier, familiar topics are offered as ways to avoid overload.
requirements: Activities must be analyzed for their cognitive demands so that guidance can target the biologically secondary components
constraints: The review warns that more passive methods can be preferable when extraneous load cannot be avoided, and that digital transfer can increase demands
target_learners: learners in activity-based and generative learning settings, including novices
target_learning_goals: protecting working memory capacity for the actual learning content during hands-on activities
examples: The review notes Fiorella and Zhang (2018) found simplifying the drawing task can have a positive effect, and Wang et al. (2023) reduced social load by having learners teach toward a webcam
key_sources: Alexander Skulmowski. (2024). Learning by Doing or Doing Without Learning? The Potentials and Challenges of Activity-Based Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09869-y

article_title: Facilitating Understanding of Movements in Dynamic Visualizations: an Embodied Perspective
citation: Björn B. de Koning & Huib K. Tabbers. (2011). Facilitating Understanding of Movements in Dynamic Visualizations: an Embodied Perspective. Educ Psychol Rev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-011-9173-8
title: Mirror neuron account: dynamic visualizations work best for human-movement tasks because observation activates the action system
description: The review reports Van Gog et al.'s explanation for when animations help: watching a human perform a task is observational learning relying on the mirror neuron system, so an animation showing human movement automatically activates the cortical circuits involved in executing that action, priming similar actions and easing processing of transient information. Animations of non-human movements do not activate the learner's action system, which the account uses to explain their weaker effectiveness. The article treats this as a plausible but speculative explanation and extends the underlying logic to non-human movements via the learner's own motor system.
requirements: Explains effectiveness differences only relative to whether depicted movements are human or non-human
constraints: The article states the argument "remains rather speculative because the exact mechanisms of how the activation of mirror neurons translates into learning benefits have yet to be identified"
target_learners: learners studying dynamic systems or processes via animation or video
target_learning_goals: understanding movements depicted in dynamic visualizations
examples: The review cites animation advantages for first-aid procedures, origami folding, and knot-tying and puzzle construction as tasks involving human movements

article_title: Systematic Review of Educational Approaches to Misinformation
citation: Rau, M. A., & Premo, A. E. (2025). Systematic Review of Educational Approaches to Misinformation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10012-8
title: Taxonomy of diagnostic misinformation features
description: The review's theory-driven axis classifies misinformation characteristics that can signal falsity into four feature types: content features (quality elements such as typos, linguistic cues, rhetorical features), source features (lack of sources, obscure or fabricated sources, reliable sources), structural features (delivery format such as URLs or clickbait), and network features (how information is obtained or distributed, e.g., spreading patterns). The authors note that "Several features can signal that a piece of information is false (Molina et al., 2021)" and use this taxonomy to code which features each intervention line targets. Only two articles in the corpus targeted network features.
requirements: A definition of misinformation must be complemented by feature knowledge for detection to be possible
constraints: Feature diagnosticity varies; nonverbal behaviors are reported as mostly unreliable cues
target_learners: learners being trained to detect misinformation
target_learning_goals: identifying misinformation via content, source, structural, and network cues
examples: Lie detection trainings targeted content features in 22 articles and structural features in 23; all 23 information-literacy articles targeted specific features
key_sources: Rau, M. A., & Premo, A. E. (2025). Systematic Review of Educational Approaches to Misinformation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10012-8

article_title: What Are Teacher–Student Relationships in Adolescent Motivation Research? A Systematic Review of Conceptualizations, Measurement, and Analysis
citation: Emma C. Burns · Penny Van Bergen. (2025). What Are Teacher–Student Relationships in Adolescent Motivation Research? A Systematic Review of Conceptualizations, Measurement, and Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09998-y
title: The Model for Interpersonal Teacher Behavior (MITB) describes teacher–student relationships via a circumplex of influence and proximity, typically measured with the QTI
description: The MITB uses a communicative systems approach in which all teacher behavior functions as nonverbal communication and students' perceptions of that behavior reflect the underlying relationship. "The MITB is presented as a circumplex model", with behavior located on two orthogonal axes: influence (perceptions of teacher behavior as controlling) and proximity (perceptions of teacher behavior as socially and academically approachable). Research typically assesses relationships via these axes, sometimes via eight octants; the most common measure is the Questionnaire on Teacher Interaction (QTI).
requirements: Consistent specification of interpersonal behaviors as relating to an individual student or multiple students, so dyadic relationships can be disentangled from broader classroom climates
constraints: QTI items framing teacher behavior as an independent observation, not in relation to students, cannot be considered equivalent to behavioral interactions with students
target_learning_goals: Understanding how teacher interpersonal behavior shapes students' perceptions of the relationship and their motivation
examples: Some MITB research aggregates relationships to the classroom level or examines them as multilevel systems

article_title: Developmental change in the influence of domain-general abilities and domain-specific knowledge on mathematics achievement: An eight-year longitudinal study.
citation: Geary David C., Nicholas Alan, Li Yaoran, Sun Jianguo. (2017). Developmental Change in the Influence of Domain-General Abilities and Domain-Specific Knowledge on Mathematics Achievement: An Eight-Year Longitudinal Study. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000159
title: Mixed functional data analysis for estimating grade-by-grade longitudinal predictor effects
description: The article applies longitudinal mixed functional data analysis (FDA) to estimate regression effects as functions of grade, using linear splines for fixed and random effect functions. It argues FDA "is not constrained by the parametric assumptions of cross-lagged and related models" and enables simultaneous estimation of overall domain-general and domain-specific effects, grade-by-grade contributions of individual variables, and linear and non-linear across-grade change in these effects on subsequent mathematics achievement.
requirements: Longitudinal data with repeated assessments across multiple grades for the outcome and predictors, standardized at each grade to a common metric.
constraints: The article notes the correlational data do not support strong causal inferences, and the relatively small sample may have reduced statistical power for some analyses.
target_learners: Children followed longitudinally from kindergarten through 8th grade
target_learning_goals: Mathematics achievement development
examples: The %fmixed SAS macro following Liu and Guo (2011) was used to fit models estimating domain-general and domain-specific effects from 2nd to 8th grade.

article_title: Effects of discipline techniques on children's personality trait inferences.
citation: Rice, W. K., Jr. (1973). Effects of Discipline Techniques on Children's Personality-Trait Inferences. Ph.D. dissertation, The University of Oklahoma. University Microfilms No. 74-12,322. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Effects+of+Discipline+Techniques+on+Children%27s+Personality-Trait+Inferences
title: Keep approval-focused desists of a negative quality to a minimum in classroom discipline
description: Because observers attribute less desirable traits to both the disciplined child and the teacher after approval-focused desists, and because self-concept is influenced by how others view a person, the authors recommend limiting this discipline technique. As they state, "it is suggested that the use of approval- focused desists of a negative quality b e  kept minimal." The recommendation rests on the laboratory finding that desist type changes how the child and teacher are viewed.
requirements: Teachers must have alternative desist forms available, such as task-focused desists that direct negative content at the activity rather than the child
constraints: The finding comes from a laboratory tape-listening setting with minimal information; the authors note that significant laboratory results frequently do not translate into significant classroom effects, and that under normal classroom conditions the covariation principle applies and different results might be obtained
target_learning_goals: maintaining a classroom climate that protects the school-self concept and peer standing of disciplined students
examples: The experiment presented eighth graders with tape-recorded approval-focused or task-focused desists and measured their trait and confidence ratings of the target child and the teacher

article_title: Certain abilities fundamental to the study of geometry.
citation: Minnick, J. H. (1925). Certain abilities fundamental to the study of geometry. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Certain+Abilities+Fundamental+to+the+Study+of+Geometry
title: Tests A, B, C, and D: four diagnostic tests for the fundamental geometry abilities
description: An element consisting of four paper-and-pencil diagnostic tests, each arranged to measure only one of the four abilities. Test A asked pupils to draw the figure for stated exercises; in Test B the figure was drawn and the pupil stated hypothesis and conclusion; in Test C a drawn figure with given facts was supplemented by as many more facts as the pupil could add; in Test D the figure, started hypothesis and conclusion, and a list of facts were given, and the pupil was asked to give the proof. Each test was given to not less than one thousand pupils in sixty-three schools.
requirements: Simple and definite directions so teachers can administer the tests uniformly; the author tried them out with high school classes and made changes before use
constraints: Two schools whose returns indicated a variation from the directions were rejected; scoring required the author to mark all papers personally to insure uniformity
target_learners: High school geometry pupils in classes that recently completed the first two books of geometry
target_learning_goals: Diagnosis of weaknesses in the abilities fundamental to geometric proof
examples: Each test yielded two scores: a positive score for correct necessary statements and a negative score for incorrect and unnecessary statements, which the author held should not be combined

article_title: A micro-genesis account of longer-form reinforcement learning in structured and unstructured environments
citation: Benjamin James Dyson and Ahad Asad. (2021). A micro-genesis account of longer-form reinforcement learning in structured and unstructured environments. npj Science of Learning 6:19. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00098-4
title: Micro-genesis account: between-task win-calmness and loss-restlessness must first develop from micro-transactions within tasks
description: The article proposes that longer-form reinforcement-learning expressions described between tasks (gain-calmness as "decreased choice switching following prior tasks producing gains" and loss-restlessness as "increased tendency to switch choices following prior tasks with losses") can only manifest across tasks if they first develop from contingencies between trial triplets within a task. It operationalises calmness as two consecutive stay responses and restlessness as two consecutive shift responses, testing whether the trial n-2 outcome shapes stay-stay or shift-shift responding. The account retains win-stay and lose-shift as central mechanisms while extending the associative chain across multiple outcomes and actions.
requirements: Participants must experience reliable gains or losses different from baseline for the longer-form effects to take effect
constraints: Effects are studied within repeated zero-sum games (Rock, Paper, Scissors) against computerised opponents
target_learners: adult participants making repeated choices in competitive decision-making games
target_learning_goals: outcome-action associative learning (win-stay/lose-shift) in repeated decision-making
examples: Calmness was coded as stay-stay across trials n-2 to n-1 and n-1 to n, and restlessness as shift-shift across the same window, analysed as a function of the trial n-2 outcome
key_sources: Benjamin James Dyson and Ahad Asad. (2021). A micro-genesis account of longer-form reinforcement learning in structured and unstructured environments. npj Science of Learning 6:19. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00098-4

article_title: What students do when encountering failure in collaborative tasks
citation: Rachel Lam. (2019). What students do when encountering failure in collaborative tasks. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0045-1
title: Micro-failures: failure conceptualized as recognizable in-process iterations of uncertainty and response during learning
description: Drawing on Tawfik, Rong, and Choi, the article adopts a process view of failure rather than a static end-product view. As the article states, they "coin the term "micro-failures," which specifically refer to iterations where a learner recognizes an uncertainty while working through a task and then has the opportunity to respond to improve understanding." Student dialogs during collaboration make these iterations visible in ways end-products like solutions cannot. The framework connects failure recognition to cognitive mechanisms of assimilation, disequilibrium/cognitive conflict, an inquiry state, and mental-model restructuring, cycling at each recognition of failure.
requirements: Tasks that implicitly surface knowledge gaps so learners can overtly display awareness of impasses, and opportunities to respond to those impasses
constraints: The framework is applied in this article to dialogs from dyadic collaboration in a single environmental-sustainability topic with fourth graders
target_learning_goals: recognizing and responding to knowledge gaps during collaborative problem solving
examples: Micro-failure episodes were operationalized as moments of overtly displayed impasse: verbalized uncertainty, disagreement, questions, long pauses, or hedges
key_sources: Rachel Lam. (2019). What students do when encountering failure in collaborative tasks. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0045-1

article_title: Constructivist developmental theory is needed in developmental neuroscience
citation: Arsalidou, M. & Pascual-Leone, J. (2016). Constructivist developmental theory is needed in developmental neuroscience. npj Science of Learning 1, 16016. https://doi.org/10.1038/npjscilearn.2016.16
title: Misleading versus facilitating tasks: misleading situations reliably assess effective complexity of mental attention
description: The article distinguishes misleading tasks, which activate mutually incompatible schemes competing for application (e.g., dual-task paradigms and backward span tasks), from facilitating tasks solvable with habitual automatised schemes, such as standard forward span tasks. Misleading situations "can assess effective complexity reliably — whereas facilitating situations, common in learning/memory paradigms and psychometric-intelligence tasks, do not". Effective complexity is indexed by the number of effortfully activated task-relevant schemes required, and these situations show developmental performance discontinuities subtending stages.
requirements: Attentional inhibition of misleading or irrelevant schemes concurrent with effortful mental activation of relevant schemes; ignoring this methodological prescription leads to errors in assessing effective complexity of tasks
constraints: Methods of task analysis for estimating complexity more theoretically are still undeveloped; the passing-age criterion remains a safe but relative estimate
target_learners: children of differing ages and ability levels
target_learning_goals: measuring mental-attentional capacity and effective task complexity
examples: Backwards digit span, where the automatised habit of saying digits forward competes with the instruction to say them backwards, exemplifies a misleading task
key_sources: Arsalidou, M. & Pascual-Leone, J. (2016). Constructivist developmental theory is needed in developmental neuroscience. npj Science of Learning 1, 16016. https://doi.org/10.1038/npjscilearn.2016.16

article_title: The method of educational assessment affects children’s neural processing and performance: behavioural and fMRI Evidence
citation: Howard, S. J., Burianová, H., Calleia, A., Fynes-Clinton, S., Kervin, L. and Bokosmaty, S. (2017). The method of educational assessment affects children's neural processing and performance: behavioural and fMRI Evidence. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0010-9
title: Design assessments to maximise variance associated with the target competencies and minimise variance from extraneous information and processing
description: A test-construction principle the article derives from its findings: because methods differ in WM demands that are peripheral to the construct, developers should prefer methods that keep WM demands essential to the target ability. The article states "it is preferable to maximise variance associated with the competencies being assessed and minimise the variance associated with any extraneous information and processing, as is the case for all test construction", so that WM exerts only its indirect effect through learning or a direct role in the target ability.
requirements: Assessment development must consider not only what to assess but also how to assess
constraints: Proofreading-type tasks may still legitimately require WM when the target ability itself requires concurrent consideration of intent, meaning and language conventions
target_learners: all test-takers of standardised educational assessments, including young children
target_learning_goals: valid and accurate indexing of competencies such as spelling, numeracy and reading comprehension
examples: The study compared three standardised spelling methods equated for word difficulty, pilot-tested with 31 Grade 2 children, showing accuracy ordering from multiple choice to proofreading

article_title: Shifting the mindset culture to address global educational disparities
citation: Hecht, C. A., Murphy, M. C., Dweck, C. S., Bryan, C. J., Trzesniewski, K. H., Medrano, F. N., Giani, M., Mhatre, P., & Yeager, D. S. (2023). Shifting the mindset culture to address global educational disparities. npj Science of Learning 8:29. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00181-y
title: Mindset classroom culture framework: messages and opportunities as two dimensions communicating a growth or fixed culture
description: This framework defines the classroom culture as "the shared system of beliefs, goals, and norms that define what it means to be a learner in that classroom," and the mindset culture as the shared beliefs about learning in a school or classroom. It holds that teachers communicate the culture through two broad, empirically identified dimensions: informal verbal messages about growth, and formal opportunities to improve such as learning-focused grading and revision for credit. The framework predicts that cultures supporting growth beliefs narrow group-based achievement disparities by providing "psychological affordances" for students' own growth mindset beliefs.
requirements: Practices must clearly and consistently lead students to perceive the teacher as endorsing a growth mindset and provide affordances for students to benefit from their own growth mindset beliefs
constraints: The article states effects of growth mindset beliefs and interventions are heterogeneous, varying across students and academic contexts, and strongest where contexts support and reinforce the intervention message
target_learners: adolescent and college students, especially those from structurally disadvantaged groups
target_learning_goals: learning-oriented behaviors, belonging, willingness to take on challenging coursework
examples: Laboratory studies manipulated teacher statements and grading policies (Table 1) and measured students' perceived culture and learning-oriented choices

article_title: Do it yourself: discerning the effects of self-directed activity on conceptual learning
citation: Brod, G., Holstein, E., Weindorf, L., Colantonio, J., Bonawitz, E. & Theobald, M. (2025). Do it yourself: discerning the effects of self-directed activity on conceptual learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00364-9
title: Even minimal volitional acts such as generating predictions support conceptual learning beyond the informational content of the evidence
description: This principle holds that letting learners perform a volitional act themselves—even one that does not alter the evidence they see, such as generating a prediction before feedback—enhances causal learning relative to observing another learner perform the same act. The article's experiment shows the benefit persists when evidence informativeness, timing, and physical activity are held constant via personalized Bayesian yoking, and links the benefit to increased perceived autonomy.
requirements: Learners must generate their own response before seeing the outcome
The observed evidence must be matched to the learner's own prior beliefs so the comparison is fair
constraints: Demonstrated with a computerized prediction-feedback task in 5- to 7-year-olds; generalization to other domains and to hands-on experimentation is untested
target_learning_goals: causal/conceptual learning and belief revision
examples: In the experiment, children in the active condition made their own predictions about which sphere would displace more water before seeing the outcome, while yoked children observed matched predictions, with all children seeing identical evidence
key_sources: Brod, G., Holstein, E., Weindorf, L., Colantonio, J., Bonawitz, E. & Theobald, M. (2025). Do it yourself: discerning the effects of self-directed activity on conceptual learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00364-9

article_title: Micro-consolidation occurs when learning an implicit motor sequence, but is not influenced by HIIT exercise
citation: Emily Brooks, Sarah Wallis, Joshua Hendrikse & James Coxon. (2024). Micro-consolidation occurs when learning an implicit motor sequence, but is not influenced by HIIT exercise. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00238-6
title: Micro-consolidation is a rapid consolidation process shared across memory systems with distinct topology, not requiring explicit sequence awareness
description: The article characterises micro-consolidation as consolidation occurring "on a more rapid scale of seconds", measurable as performance gains during brief rest periods between practice blocks. Because the effect appeared in an implicit task supported by cortico-striatal networks, whereas earlier evidence came from explicit tasks implicating hippocampal-neocortical replay, the authors propose "micro-consolidation as a process shared across memory systems with distinct topology". Explicit sequence awareness is not required for the effect to occur.
requirements: Alternating practice and rest structure (10-s epochs) with skill quantified as correct responses per second, as in the original Bonstrup paradigm
constraints: Demonstrated here for an implicit 12-item fixed sequence in healthy young adults; whether there is overlap with explicit micro-consolidation mechanisms remains open
target_learners: healthy young adults learning novel motor sequences
target_learning_goals: early-phase implicit motor sequence skill acquisition
examples: Thirty-eight adults performed an implicit serial reaction time task alternating 10-s practice and rest for 16 blocks, with micro-offline gains modelling early learning

article_title: Both individual and peer growth mindsets matter for academic resilience
citation: King, R.B., Li, J., & Wang, Y. (2026). Both individual and peer growth mindsets matter for academic resilience. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00403-z
title: Mindset-by-context framework: growth mindsets as a "seed" that grows in a social context serving as "soil"
description: The mindset-by-context framework holds that an individual's growth mindset operates within a social environment that can reinforce or undermine it. The article states that "an individual's growth mindset is like a 'seed' that grows in the social context, which serves as the 'soil'", and that "A supportive context is a prerequisite for sustaining the benefits of an individual's growth mindset". Fixed-mindset school ecologies with practices such as emphasizing performance feedback may weaken mindset effects. The study's interaction finding is offered as empirical fleshing-out of this framework.
requirements: For growth mindsets to have maximal effect, the broader environment must be congruent with the individual's beliefs
constraints: Peer mindset was operationalized only at school level; classroom-level context was not measurable in PISA
target_learning_goals: academic achievement and resilience under socioeconomic adversity
key_sources: King, R.B., Li, J., & Wang, Y. (2026). Both individual and peer growth mindsets matter for academic resilience. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00403-z

article_title: Divergent effects of mindsets on performance trajectories
citation: Melody M. Chao, Allen H. Huang, Anirban Mukhopadhyay & Janghoon Shon. (2025). Divergent effects of mindsets on performance trajectories. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00355-w
title: Growth versus fixed mindset as opposite ends of a continuum within an achievement-motivation model
description: The article treats mindsets as beliefs about the malleability of personal attributes arranged on a continuum, with "the fixed and growth mindsets conceptualized as opposite ends of a continuum, ranging from a relatively rigid and immutable view of personal attributes to a dynamic view of change". The growth mindset "is built on a model of achievement motivation", premised on beliefs shaping how individuals respond to challenges and setbacks, motivating persistence. The study tests this framework's implicit linearity assumption and finds it fails.
requirements: A mindset measure capturing endorsement of beliefs in growth and change along the continuum, as the article's 3-item scale did
constraints: The article's own data contradict the framework's assumed linear positive association between growth mindset strength and performance
target_learning_goals: academic achievement and persistence through challenge

article_title: Growth mindset and socioeconomic inequality in academic achievement across seventy-three PISA countries

description: Based on the finding that growth mindset mediates only about 2.9–3.2% of the SES effect, the article recommends that "interventions solely focused on cultivating this individual-level trait may have a limited impact on reducing educational inequalities". It argues greater emphasis and resources should be directed toward systemic factors such as school resources, teacher quality, and parental involvement, which the study implies may play a more substantial role in equitable outcomes.

description: The article's central explanatory account is that support for collaborative learning has evolved from static scripted collaboration (structured interfaces, prompts, scripted roles) toward adaptive, context-sensitive support. This "novel type of micro-script support for productive discussion processes" is "enabled by an integration of text mining and conversational agents". Automatic analysis of collaborative processes enables real-time assessment, dynamically triggered interventions during sessions, and efficient analysis of collaborative learning interactions.

citation: Hall, L., Tazzyman, S., Hume, C., Endrass, B., Lim, M.-Y., Hofstede, G., Paiva, A., Andre, E., Kappas, A., & Aylett, R. (2014). Learning to Overcome Cultural Conflict through Engaging with Intelligent Agents in Synthetic Cultures. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0031-y
title: MIXER experiential learning application
description: MIXER (Moderating Interactions for Cross-Cultural Empathic Relationships) is a computer-based learning experience for 9–11 year olds set in a virtual summer camp where two teams of six intelligent agents play Werewolves with different rule sets representing two synthetic cultures or moral circles. The child user acts as an invisible friend advising the protagonist Tom via a tablet-based Pictorial Interaction Language of over 70 graphics, learning by observing and advising rather than playing. The scenario ends with Tom resolving the conflict by discussing the rule differences, reinforcing that apparent unfairness may reflect simple differences that can be resolved.
requirements: Delivery as part of a whole learning experience with teacher-led classroom discussion to reinforce the message that difference is acceptable
constraints: Does not attempt to create believable cultural differences between the groups other than the rule sets, given the target group's age and experience
target_learning_goals: intercultural conflict competence
willingness to include out-group members in one's moral circle
examples: Children interacted with MIXER on a laptop with headphones and the Pictorial Interaction Language on an iPad, in small groups leaving the classroom

citation: Luis Alberto Pinos Ullauri, Alexis Lebis, Abir Karami, Mathieu Vermeulen, Anthony Fleury, Wim Van den Noortgate. (2025). A Recommender System of Postgraduate Courses Based on Soft Skills: A Psychometric-inspired Approach. Int J Artif Intell Educ 35. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00463-z
title: MIRT-inspired fitness aggregation: compensatory average and partially compensatory product over per-skill scores
description: To turn the multi-objective problem of optimising 10 per-skill scores into a mono-objective one, the article proposes two aggregation methods inspired by Multidimensional Item Response Theory. The compensatory method averages the scores, allowing "compensation between surpluses or deficits of soft skill proficiency"; the partially compensatory method multiplies them, requiring each score to be as high as possible. The article states this approach is "inspired from Multidimensional Item Response Theory (MIRT)", which allows treating the problem as mono-objective and potentially diminishing optimisation complexity.
requirements: Per-skill scores scaled to the range between zero and one
A targeted soft skill profile defining the thresholds against which discrepancies are scored
constraints: Percentage increases are not comparable across aggregation methods because of their different mathematical definitions
target_learning_goals: balancing proficiency across multiple soft skills relative to targets
examples: With compensatory aggregation a 10% increase in each of 10 scores conveys a 10% fitness increase, whereas in partially compensatory aggregation it translates to 159.4%

article_title: An Intelligent Support System to Help Teachers Plan Field Trips
citation: Noemi Mauro, Liliana Ardissono, Federica Cena, Livio Scarpinati, Gianluca Torta. (2024). An Intelligent Support System to Help Teachers Plan Field Trips. Int J Artif Intell Educ 34, 793–824. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00366-x
title: Mixed-initiative interaction for field trip planning: user control combined with delegated scheduling support
description: The article's organizing framework applies Horvitz's mixed-initiative interaction to field trip organization: the teacher leads every design step and selects places and activities, while the system takes over burdensome computations such as consistency checks and itinerary optimization. Unlike most personalized tour planners that autonomously generate optimized itineraries and let users only critique complete solutions, this approach combines information filtering with automated scheduling so that "the user [is] in full control of the design process, delegating the system to manage difficult and burdensome tasks such as consistency checks and itinerary optimization". The framework treats PoIs as complex entities aggregating activities, and separates information filtering from itinerary optimization, which is solved as a Travelling Salesman Problem rather than a utility-maximizing Tourist Trip Design Problem.
requirements: An underlying itinerary generation service that computes the schedule taking the shortest time, so feasibility annotations rest on an optimized partial schedule
constraints: The approach excludes automated planning where the system leads the construction of the itinerary, and does not focus on fine-grained routing or reactive itinerary adaptation during trip execution
target_learners: Teachers of any school level organizing field trips for whole classes
target_learning_goals: Design of out-of-school learning itineraries aligned with didactic objectives and time constraints
examples: Free-text comments showed participants appreciated the mixed-initiative model, e.g., liking "the automatic planning function, so that you don't have to build the itinerary manually, but still have the ability to select the activities to do"
key_sources: Noemi Mauro, Liliana Ardissono, Federica Cena, Livio Scarpinati, Gianluca Torta. (2024). An Intelligent Support System to Help Teachers Plan Field Trips. Int J Artif Intell Educ 34, 793–824. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00366-x

article_title: Young children’s embodied interactions with a social robot
citation: Yanghee Kim · Michael Tscholl. (2021). Young children's embodied interactions with a social robot. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09978-3
title: Minimalistic design: tap into children's natural way of embodied interaction rather than assigning tasks or giving direct instructions
description: The authors propose a form of minimalistic design for young children that aligns with a child's world and habitual way of embodied interaction. In their triadic activity, the robot introduced itself as a newbie from another planet who needed help, and its simple remarks such as "I like that" and "I'm confused" functioned as powerful feedback prompting children to discuss and redo the activity. The design demonstrated that intense embodied engagement was elicited without direct instructions or task assignment.
requirements: The robot's embodied social behavior must trigger task-related behavior and relevant feedback, as in the newbie persona and simple evaluative remarks
constraints: The authors frame this from observations of children aged three to six interacting freely over time; current natural language processing is not sufficiently mature to manage natural conversations, so a Wizard of Oz method controlled the robot's utterances
target_learners: young children in early childhood and kindergarten settings
target_learning_goals: early literacy and arithmetic skills
collaborative communication skills
early science concepts
examples: The robot being new to earth signaled to children that they had to help it; its remark "I'm confused" when children conflicted prompted them to re-do the activity and agree on one answer

article_title: Safeguarding student privacy in an age of analytics
citation: Royce Kimmons. (2021). Safeguarding student privacy in an age of analytics. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09950-1
title: Start learning analytics with data types that introduce minimal risk to students and are well-connected to the system's intended learning objectives
description: The article recommends that ethical learning analytics design should not treat all data uniformly but begin by selecting data types that pose little risk to students while serving the system's purpose. It states that professionals "should start by identifying and using data types that introduce minimal risk to students" that are also "reasonably well-connected to the intended purpose and learning objectives of the system."
requirements: Student voices should be involved in decision making regarding learning analytics systems.
constraints: An omnibus approach wherein all types of data are treated with equal levels of privacy consideration is overly simplistic.
target_learners: students whose data are used in learning analytics systems
target_learning_goals: ethical use of student data in learning analytics systems
examples: The recommendation is drawn from Ifenthaler and Schumacher's (2016) survey findings on differing student privacy sensitivity across data types.

citation: Victoria Abramenka-Lachheb, Gamze Ozogul. (2025). Interaction analysis of learning objects in online courses: What are their interactive characteristics and design intent behind them? Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10556-0
title: Minimize attention demand of interactive learning objects so learners can focus on authentic tasks
description: Because authentic learning tasks inherently require higher-order thinking, the article recommends that interactive learning objects minimize unnecessary cognitive strain: "Designers should focus on making navigation and interaction intuitive so that learners can fully engage with the content and tasks rather than being burdened by complex interface mechanics." requirements: Navigation and interaction must be intuitive; external coders advised that attention demand should remain low from a technology perspective so students focus on the authentic task itself
constraints: Recommendation arises in the context of authentic learning tasks in online higher education courses

Transfer of school knowledge to work practice
