citation: Ozcelik, E., Ercil Cagiltay, N., & Sahin Ozcelik, N. (2013). The effect of uncertainty on learning in game-like environments. Computers & Education, 67, 12–20. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2013.02.009
title: Mission 336: a game-like learning environment for Entity-Relationship Diagrams with an uncertain and a certain version
description: Mission 336 is a computer-based game-like learning tool developed to teach Entity-Relationship Diagram concepts in higher education software engineering programs. Players "collect 336 points" by answering true–false questions about ER diagrams across seven conceptual doors, earning "ten points and the total value of the dice" for correct answers. Two versions were built: an uncertain version with random dice values and a certain version yielding double 3, identical otherwise in content and interface.

constraints: The two versions differ only in dice values; the certain version yields a fixed double-3 throw with no randomness
target_learners: undergraduate students in computer engineering, software engineering, and information systems engineering
target_learning_goals: Entity-Relationship Diagram concepts including entities, attributes, keys, cardinality, participation, and relationship types
examples: Participants rolled two dice, answered true–false statements about ER diagrams, and received feedback with points gained or lost

description: Miller's pyramid is a four-level framework ordering assessment targets from factual knowledge to real-world performance: "Knows" (best assessed with written exams), "Knows How" (written or oral exams), "Shows How" (performance-based assessments with standardized simulations or oral exams with standardized scenarios), and "Does" (clinic-based performance assessments). procedural skills
communication skills
clinical performance
examples: The review mapped the 92 identified assessments onto the pyramid, finding performance-based assessments correspond to the Does and Shows How levels

Delivery by rheumatology specialists rather than only adjacent specialties
constraints: Cross-sectional evidence base; the review notes results may not represent current teaching levels

career awareness of rheumatology
examples: The review's included studies reported dedicated rheumatology hours ranging from 4 to 120 h per student

description: The review proposes that dementia care competencies operate at three system levels. article_title: Assessing the patient safety competencies of healthcare professionals: a systematic review.
citation: Okuyama Ayako, Martowirono Kartinie, Bijnen Bart. (2011). Assessing the patient safety competencies of healthcare professionals: a systematic review. BMJ Quality & Safety. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3203526/
title: Miller's four competency levels as an organising framework for patient safety assessment
description: The review uses Miller's four competency levels — 'knows', 'knows how', 'shows how', and 'does' — as its central organising framework for categorising assessment tools. At each level "the trainee should be able to demonstrate the ability to imitate or replicate a protocol, apply principles in a familiar situation, adapt principles to new situations, and associate new knowledge with previously learned principles". constraints: Competence is context dependent and can only be assessed in the work place.

positive attitude toward learning English

title: Mind Maps as hierarchical visual organization of knowledge (Ozbel/Ausubel-based account)
description: The article presents the Mind Map as an application of Ozbel theory, which assumed that the learner's brain stores information in sequential hierarchy from general to specific to facilitate learning and retrieval. New information joins an existing knowledge structure and integrates to become part of the total structure, which can be presented in one chart called a Mind Map. Components include a main idea or concept, connective words, horizontal links, and examples. The article uses this account to justify teaching Arabic grammar concepts through colorful hierarchical charts that stimulate attention.
requirements: Full learning requires that the material structure be organized clearly and related to the new material, linking what a learner knows with what he learns
constraints: The account is presented as theoretical background attributed to Attiyah (2008) and Buzan (2007), not as a tested result of this study

title: The brain break: a daily focused-attention core practice implemented four times daily with scaffolds for preschoolers
description: The brain break is the core practice of the MindUP curriculum: "a brief focused attention activity that teachers implement in their classroom with their students four times daily—usually at the start of the day, after recess, after lunch, and at the end of the day." title: Minute-by-minute whole-classroom observation protocol for student behavior and classroom context
description: The authors developed a classroom observation approach that uses time sampling to observe all children minute by minute, replacing the prior focal-child approach in which each child was observed only 2-6 minutes. The protocol "documents student behavior (off-task, disruptive, aggressive and social isolation), classroom context (instructional format, subject area), overall level of classroom behavior (a classroom scan every 5 minutes) and teachers' instructional and classroom management style (punitive, neutral, positive)". It was used in the GBG professional development trial in Houston.
requirements: Trained observers achieving high percentage agreement; the article reports observers reached 80% or higher agreement
constraints: Developed for and reported on the first cohort of the GBG PD Models trial in Houston Independent School District; impact analysis was not yet conducted
target_learners: first- and second-grade students in elementary classrooms
target_learning_goals: accurate measurement of aggressive, disruptive, off-task and socially isolated classroom behavior
examples: Students were observed in 5 minute segments, averaging 43.8 minutes in the morning and 41.1 minutes in the afternoon during fall observations

article_title: Investigating the Effectiveness of Group Work in Mathematics
citation: Anastasia Sofroniou and Konstantinos Poutos. (2016). Investigating the Effectiveness of Group Work in Mathematics. Educ. Sci. 2016, 6, 30. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci6030030
title: Mixed-caliber group work with student-set problems and peer marking in tutorial sessions
description: The article's group work setup paired weaker and stronger students together, never forming groups solely of weak students, and alternated lecturer-set problems with problems devised by group members for fellow groups to tackle. After completion, solutions were returned to the posing group "to mark and provide appropriate feedback to their peers", so students deepened their understanding while learning to communicate, deliberate, assess and improve their mistakes.
requirements: The educator specifies academic objectives, makes instructional decisions such as group size and duration, and clarifies the task and assignment goals
Groups contain a mixture of student calibers
constraints: The article notes group work can be nonproductive if only one member does all the work, and less capable members may leave work to others
target_learners: first-year university engineering students in mathematics tutorials
target_learning_goals: deepen understanding of a challenging mathematics topic
develop communication, deliberation and assessment skills
examples: Over four weeks of twice-weekly one-hour tutorials on integration (substitution, parts, partial fractions, civil engineering applications), students worked in mixed pairs, posed problems to other groups, and marked peers' solutions with feedback.

title: Gardner's Multiple Intelligences Theory as a cognitive-and-emotional framework for designing Technology lessons
description: The article uses Gardner's Multiple Intelligences Theory (MIT) as the organizing framework: intelligence is not limited to its cognitive facet but includes affective and emotional sides, and each student has a prevalent Intelligence Style (IS). The authors operationalise MIT by designing a Didactic Unit with nine activities, one oriented to each IS, and by testing whether attending to IS improves both emotional yield and content acquisition. As they write, the theory "does not limit intelligence to its purely cognitive facet" but takes account of "its affective and emotional sides".
requirements: Students' prevalent IS must be identified (here via a 32-item questionnaire adapted from Armstrong/Giorgis) so activities can be matched to styles
constraints: The article notes it is difficult to find specific educative applications of the theory despite its age
target_learners: Secondary school students, ages 12-13, Technology and Design lessons
target_learning_goals: Technology content acquisition (materials, structures, electricity, computing)
positive emotional engagement with Technology
examples: The intervention group carried out nine activities, e.g. students with musical prevalent intelligence could find out or compose a song about the electromagnetic field

article_title: Comparative Effect of Memory and Cognitive Strategies Training on EFL Intermediate Learners' Vocabulary Learning
citation: Maryam Banisaeid. (2013). Comparative Effect of Memory and Cognitive Strategies Training on EFL Intermediate Learners' Vocabulary Learning. English Language Teaching, 6(8). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n8p108
title: Mix memory and cognitive strategy training in the vocabulary syllabus rather than teaching only one category
description: The article recommends that vocabulary programs combine both strategy categories in overt training. It argues that "strategy training should be mixed in the syllabus of the educational program" because the two categories serve complementary purposes, learners gain knowledge of more strategies, and learners can choose strategies fitting their style and purposes. The recommendation rests on the study's strategy-use findings and the null word-learning comparison.
requirements: Overt, explicit training so learners understand the strategies for future use
At least 3 to 4 hours study on each specific strategy, per Cohen (2003) as cited in the article
constraints: Evidence base is one quasi-experiment with 60 intermediate female learners; no word-learning advantage was shown for either category

target_learning_goals: vocabulary learning
strategic self-directed vocabulary learning
examples: One group trained with keyword and semantic map, the other with repetition and flashcards, over 11 sessions using English Book 1 and ten-page strategy pamphlets

article_title: The Impact of Teaching Oriental Music Using Blended Learning Approach
citation: Chamila Nishanthi Edward, David Asirvatham & Md Gapar Md Johar. (2019). The Impact of Teaching Oriental Music Using Blended Learning Approach. Malaysian Journal of Learning and Instruction, 16(1), 81-103. https://mjli.uum.edu.my
title: Mixed objectivist and constructivist instructional design model for intensive blended courses
description: The article applies an instructional design model that combines objectivist features (teacher-led face-to-face instruction, defined learning goals, structured lesson plans, assessment aligned with goals) with constructivist features (student-controlled Moodle platforms, group activities for knowledge construction, new media integration, self-assessments). The authors state that "a mixed instructional design model combining both the features of objectivist and constructivist methods of instructing and learning would be a distinctive strategy to be utilized for intensive BL course". The model structured the blended Oriental Music course tested in the experiment.
requirements: Requires both objectivist structured instruction and constructivist student-controlled online activities to be combined in one course design
constraints: Recommended for intensive blended courses where lesson time is limited, per the article's context of music lessons with limited allocated time

examples: Table 1 lists the objectivist features (teacher led face-to-face instructions, lecture demonstrations) and constructivist features (student controlled online learning platforms (Moodle), group activities for knowledge construction) used in the music practical and theory lessons

title: Mind map technique as a visual, associative learning technique engaging multiple cortical skills
description: The mind map technique, developed by Tony Buzan as a note-taking technique, is described as a 2-dimensional visual display in which a keyword or visual sits at the center and associations progress laterally with different colors, symbols, and shapes. The article presents it as supporting "the natural thought process where all cortical skills , including word, i mage, number, logic, rhythm, color , and spatial awareness skills , are simultaneously used". In this study it was used as a comprehensive teaching-learning material in volleyball lessons, with students creating mind maps each class and receiving regular feedback.
requirements: Learners determine the main points of the material hierarchically, establish connections among concepts, and create a framed form
Good dialogue between teacher and student, since every student expresses associations in a different way
constraints: Mind maps may pose a time problem and might not be suitable for every course or every topic
target_learners: 6th-grade secondary school students in physical education
target_learning_goals: Cognitive domain knowledge of the volleyball unit
Psychomotor volleyball skills (overhand pass, bump pass, underhand serve)
examples: Students in the experimental group were introduced to the technique for 40 minutes, then created mind maps in every new class across a 9-week volleyball unit

title: MI Inventory (Gardner/Harms, Turkish adaptation) and researcher-developed 19-item success test
description: Two data-collection instruments. The MI inventory, developed by Gardner, improved by Harms, translated by Oral (2001) and adjusted by Kanat (2008), "involved totally 10 items for each intelligence field overall 80 items" scored 1–5, with Cronbach Alpha 0.834. The success test, developed by the researchers with expert review and a table of specification, retained "totally 19 questions in its final version" after pilot testing, with KR-20 of 0.84; it served as both success test and, reapplied three weeks later, permanence test.
requirements: Expert review and a table of specification for content validity
Pilot testing with item discrimination screening (items with discrimination under 0.30 excluded)
constraints: Developed for 8th-grade visual arts content on miniature pictures
target_learning_goals: measuring success and permanence of visual arts knowledge
examples: Each question scored 1 point if correct, 0 if blank, wrong, or multi-chosen

description: The intervention artifact is a computerized educational package "selected from the packages prepared by ministry of education as part of Intel program ; education for future". constraints: The package was re-arbitrated by experts outside the educational administration before use

article_title: Mind the Teachers! The Impact of Mindfulness Training on Self-Regulation and Classroom Performance in a Sample of German School Teachers
citation: Rupprecht, S., Paulus, P. & Walach, H. (2017). Mind the teachers! The impact of mindfulness training on self-regulation and classroom performance in a sample of German school teacher. European Journal of Educational Research, 6(4), 565-581. https://doi.org/10.12973/eu-jer.6.4.565
title: Mindfulness as a foundation for healthy teacher self-regulation: the MBSR logic model
description: The article frames mindful awareness as "a foundation for healthy self -regulation" and models MBSR's effects through a logic model in which training builds mindful presence and mindful acceptance, which in turn improve teacher wellbeing, self-regulation ability and professional performance. Mindfulness is defined as the ability to pay purposeful, non-judgmental attention to the present moment, and mindful acceptance is distinguished from resistance or avoidance of negative emotions, which can prolong them. The mediation results are read as support for this pathway.
requirements: Teachers must commit to regular home practice; participants were asked to practice 40 minutes of formal meditation on six days per week in the standard programme
constraints: The pathway was tested in a small, self-selected, mostly female, non-randomized sample; a randomized follow-up study is stated to be required before results can be considered confirmed
target_learning_goals: teacher self-regulation
stress coping
emotion regulation
professional performance
examples: The study delivered an adapted 5-week MBSR curriculum (four 2.5-hour evenings and two 8-hour days, 26 hours total) and assessed the logic model's outcomes at pre-test, post-test and 3-month follow-up with questionnaires and qualitative interviews.

Teachers help students find materials and information for project creation

sensitivity to environmental problems

citation: Craig Jenkins. (2015). Poem Generator: A comparative quantitative evaluation of a microworlds-based learning approach for teaching English. International Journal of Education and Development using Information and Communication Technology, 11(2), 153-167. http://ijedict.dec.uwi.edu/viewarticle.php?id=1972
title: Microworlds-based guided discovery learning approach
description: A learning approach originating with Papert's LOGO and Turtle Graphics, in which learners acquire knowledge in a natural way through immersion in a simplified, specially designed computer environment. As Resnick puts it, "microworlds are simplified worlds, specially designed to highlight (and make accessible) particular concepts and particular ways of thinking". Rieber articulates it as guided discovery, in which the nature of the learning activity is naturally constrained by the parameters of the microworld. This article implements the approach in the subject domain of English via the Poem Generator microworld.
requirements: Microworlds need to be understandable to the learner; block-based programming addresses syntactic difficulties of textual languages, providing a low floor and ease of access
constraints: Pea (1984) suggested it may be the guidance provided by the enthusiastic teacher, not the microworld per se, that leads to improved outcomes; this study's intervention was led by one enthusiastic subject-specialist teacher
target_learners: school learners in formal classroom settings
target_learning_goals: domain concepts (mathematical ideas, written English, computational thinking) developed through exploratory programming within bounded environments
examples: Papert's Turtle Graphics for mathematics; Sharples' PAT word pattern generator for written English; the Poem Generator for poetic thinking

constraints: Observation of learners in practice suggests that they were treating the practice tasks rather mechanically

examples: A tutorial version of the mini-game lacking time pressure and reward systems with immediate CF, and a full version with time pressure, rewarding, between-learner competition, and vivid CF

Activities and tasks varied across intelligence types to address individual differences

title: MI-based speaking training program with speaking skills pre-posttest for pre-service EFL teachers

Two trained raters scoring with a shared rubric for inter-rater reliability

examples: The oral presentation test took the form of a week of continuous interviews and video recording to determine each student's actual performance level before training.

description: The MIND (Microlearning AI-Integrated Instructional Design) Model is a non-linear instructional design model grounded in TPACK and the FIL framework, with Situational Awareness incorporated into TPACK as SATPACK. It uniquely separates the delivery stage from the receiving stage to emphasise active learning, and integrates assessment of individual learning outcomes alongside evaluation of course quality. The article states, "The model consists of six stages: Analysis stage, design stage, delivery stage, receiving stage, and assessment & evaluation stage", and describes it as cost-effective, time-efficient, and adaptable across formal, non-formal, and informal settings.
requirements: Educator preparedness is addressed in the analysis stage, including any required professional development; identified needs should remain within course scope and align with institutional policies
constraints: Certain stages can be adapted to setting; for example, assessment may remain essential in formal contexts but could be optional or modified in non-formal and informal learning
target_learners: adult and lifelong learners across formal, non-formal, and informal settings
target_learning_goals: knowledge acquisition, comprehension, and knowledge application in AI-assisted research skills
examples: One educator designed the 12-module course Mastering AI-Powered Research Skills following the MIND model, using ChatGPT, Napkin AI, Gamma, NoteBookLM, and CapCut, delivered via the OpenLearning platform

title: Midterm grades as an early, theory-driven proxy for academic integration in student persistence frameworks
description: The article positions formative midterm assessment not merely as performance data but as a pedagogical checkpoint within persistence frameworks. title: Middle childhood as a period of relative plasticity in socio-emotional cognition
description: The article proposes that socio-emotional cognition in middle childhood remains relatively plastic and responsive to short, low-intensity training. Building on the account that middle childhood is "a sensitive period for the development of socio-emotional cognition", supported by continuing maturation of face-processing and mentalizing networks, the authors argue that even a 10-week observational and inferential activity can shift emotion recognition and ToM performance. They further suggest that younger children's skills "may be more rapidly developing at this age, leading to greater learning and transfer", though this remains to be replicated.

target_learning_goals: Development of emotion recognition and theory of mind skills
examples: The Year 3-only far-transfer pattern was interpreted as possibly reflecting a developmental window of enhanced learning, with potential for informing education policy in schools

title: Mindset-by-context framework: mindsets depend on whether the social context supports their deployment
description: The mindset-by-context framework holds that psychological beliefs such as growth mindsets "do not exist in a vacuum" and that whether they facilitate learning depends on whether the context supports their deployment. Walton and Yeager's seed-and-soil analogy treats the growth mindset as a seed and the social environment as the soil needed for it to flourish. constraints: The article notes the framework has been operationalized in other ways too, such as parents' mindsets, teachers' beliefs and peer norms, which this study did not examine.

intrinsic motivation
academic engagement
examples: Yeager et al. (2019) found growth mindset interventions were most effective when peers also embraced the mindset, as cited by the article.

title: Take-home mini box trainer with marked and unmarked rope exercises for laparoscopic bowel length estimation
description: A low-cost take-home training apparatus built from a plexiglass Alphatron Surgical box trainer without a camera, fitted with two laparoscopic graspers, holding a 3-meter rope fixed at its starting point to simulate Treitz's ligament. constraints: The box trainer does not use a laparoscopic camera; graspers and cord are manipulated under direct sight, excluding camera magnification and giving 3D instead of 2D sight
target_learning_goals: laparoscopic small bowel length measurement accuracy
examples: Residents trained at least once, preferably three times, for at least 15 minutes per week for two weeks with the mini box trainer exercises

article_title: Microlearning and online simulation-based virtual consultation training module for the undergraduate medical curriculum - a preliminary evaluation.
citation: Liew Siaw Cheok, Tan Maw Pin, Breen Emer, Krishnan Kuhan, Sivarajah Inthirani, Raviendran Nivashinie, Aung Thidar, Nimir Amal, Pallath Vinod. (2023). Microlearning and online simulation-based virtual consultation training module for the undergraduate medical curriculum – a preliminary evaluation. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04777-1
title: Microlearning instructional phase preceding simulation-based experiential practice with feedback
description: The module's delivery pattern pairs an asynchronous microlearning phase (weeks 1–2) with a synchronous experiential phase (weeks 3–5). Microlearning delivers "small bite-sized lessons and activities" at the learner's convenience, building foundational knowledge and confidence before practical sessions. The experiential phase then provides facilitated simulated-patient practice in groups of five or six, weekly one-on-one deliberate practice, and immediate feedback from peers, facilitators, and simulated patients, culminating in an assessed consultation.
requirements: Learners need basic prior skills in patient–doctor communication, history taking, and physical examination before entering the module
constraints: The authors state the real test of independent, unsupervised VC clinical practice is beyond this study's scope, and long-term effects remain unexamined
target_learners: Senior clinical-phase medical students and fresh graduates
target_learning_goals: Acquisition of synchronous virtual consultation skills and self-efficacy for conducting virtual consultations
examples: Nine microlearning videos across two weeks followed by three weekly 1.5-h facilitated group sessions with simulated patients, then an individual 25-min deliberate practice consultation with immediate SP feedback

article_title: Mirror training device improves dental students' performance on virtual simulation dental training system.
citation: Chu Fengqing, Zheng Jue, Wang Qirui, Lu Xiaoqing, Chen Yue, Zhong Yi, Li Yingyi, Shi Jiali, Jiang Yue, Zhang Wei, Liu Laikui, Sun Wen. (2023). Mirror training device improves dental students' performance on virtual simulation dental training system. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04300-6
title: Mirrosistant: a low-cost dental mirror training device enabling three-dimensional indirect-vision practice
description: Mirrosistant is a redesigned version of the Mirroprep device, rebuilt "with a higher rearmost wall" so objects on the screen are seen only through the mirror, which "enables the mirror training device to conduct three-dimensional movements". It supports two training sessions: tracing and filling G. V. Black cavity-classification shapes, and preparing a specified figure on raw eggs with a handpiece under indirect vision. The authors describe it as easy to operate and install, with low maintenance cost and materials obtainable in daily life.
requirements: A dental mirror and the device's screened U-profile structure so the object is visible only via indirect vision
Training sessions of prescribed shapes and raw-egg preparation tasks completed within 60 min each
constraints: Mirrosistant has only two reflecting angles (vertical and facing), incapable of simulating additional reflection angles existing in clinical procedures
target_learning_goals: indirect-vision mirror operation skills
hand–eye coordination and spatial perception in dental procedures
examples: Students traced the edge and filled in the blank of G. V. Black's classification of cavities, then prepared a specified figure on raw eggs, where too-shallow tracing left shell and too-deep tracing perforated it

article_title: Thoracic ultrasound competence for ultrasound-guided pleural procedures.
citation: McCracken DJ, Laursen CB, Barker G, Gleeson FV, Cullen KM, Rahman NM. (2019). Thoracic ultrasound competence for ultrasound-guided pleural procedures. European Respiratory Review. https://doi.org/10.1183/16000617.0090-2019
title: Miller's pyramid of competence as a framework for assessing clinical ultrasound competence
description: Miller's pyramid, first described in 1990, defines conceptual levels of clinical competence that progress from "knows" to "knows how" to "shows how" and finally to "does", each of which may be individually assessed. The review uses it as its organizing framework: written assessments best examine "knows" or "knows how", objective structured clinical examinations assess "shows how", and logbooks may strengthen validity for "does" if used robustly. It underpins the review's argument that multimodal assessment is required to cover every facet of competence.
requirements: Assessment methods must be matched to the pyramid level being measured, with multimodal tools covering all levels
constraints: The review notes minimum numbers of procedures or scans for the 'does' level remain undefined and may not be a valuable metric given learning-curve variation
target_learning_goals: procedural competence in ultrasound-guided pleural intervention
examples: The review maps written assessments, OSCEs and logbooks to the 'knows', 'shows how' and 'does' levels respectively when analysing current UK TUS assessment
key_sources: McCracken DJ, Laursen CB, Barker G, Gleeson FV, Cullen KM, Rahman NM. (2019). Thoracic ultrasound competence for ultrasound-guided pleural procedures. European Respiratory Review. https://doi.org/10.1183/16000617.0090-2019
